plan-a-website-people-can-use.title: How to plan a website people can use
plan-a-website-people-can-use.excerpt: Before you pick a single colour, write down who visits, what they came for and the one thing each page should help them do.
content: Most sites start with a colour, a logo or a template. The ones that work start with a list of the people who will visit, and what each of them came to do.
Start with the visits, not the pages
Write down the five most common reasons someone lands on your site. A bakery might hear: what is open today, can I order a cake, where do I park. Each reason becomes a page, or a section of one.
A page that tries to sell, explain and hire at the same time does none of them well. Pick the one thing a visitor should do next, and make that the biggest button.
Name the page's one job in a sentence.
Put the answer to the visitor's question first.
End with the next step as a button.
Cut anything that does not serve the job.
Test it with one real person
Ask a friend to find something on your site while you watch, without helping. Wherever they hesitate, the page needs work. Fix that, then ask someone else.

five-small-changes-faster-pages.title: Five small changes that make pages faster
five-small-changes-faster-pages.excerpt: Smaller images, fewer fonts and one less plugin. None of them takes more than ten minutes.
content: A page that appears in one second feels calm. One that takes four feels broken, however good it looks. These five changes each take a few minutes.
Resize photos before you upload them: 2000 pixels wide is plenty.
Use one font family, in two weights at most.
Remove the plugins you no longer use.
Put video on its own page, not on the homepage.
Turn on a caching plugin, or ask your host if they cache for you.
Open your homepage on your phone, away from your desk's fast connection, and count. Then make one change and count again. Small numbers add up.

colours-your-visitors-can-read.title: Choosing colours your visitors can read
colours-your-visitors-can-read.excerpt: Contrast is not a matter of taste. Here is how to check it, and what to do when your brand colour fails.
content: Light grey text on white looks elegant on a big screen and disappears in sunlight. Good contrast is what lets everyone read your site, wherever they are.
Body text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background, and large headings at least 3 to 1. Any online contrast checker tells you the ratio of two colours.
Keep it for large things: buttons, headings and backgrounds. Use a darker shade of it for links and small text, so the page still feels like yours.

corner-bakery-online-orders.title: How a corner bakery doubled its online orders
corner-bakery-online-orders.excerpt: A clearer menu page, an order button in the header and photos taken on a phone at opening time.
content: The bakery on the corner had a site that looked fine and sold almost nothing. Three changes over one weekend doubled its online orders in a month.
The menu had been a photo of the chalkboard. Now it is a page with every bread, its price and the days it is baked, so people can search it.
An order button that never moves
The header now holds a button that says Order for pickup, on every page. Nobody has to look for it.
The owner takes one photo each morning, on her phone, when the light is best and the shelves are full. People order what they can see.

what-is-new-this-autumn.title: What is new in Yantra this autumn
what-is-new-this-autumn.excerpt: Edit any part of your site by clicking it, a reading progress bar for long posts, and six palettes to start from.
content: This season's update is about doing more with fewer clicks. Here is what changed.
In the Customizer, click any part of the page, such as the logo, the menu or the footer, and its settings open.
Long posts can show a thin bar at the top of the window that fills as you read.
Indigo, Ocean, Forest, Ember, Rose and Graphite each set every colour on the site in one go, all with readable contrast.

button-labels-say-what-happens.title: Button labels that say what happens next
button-labels-say-what-happens.excerpt: Submit tells nobody anything. Name the action, and keep the same word from the button to the message after it.
content: A button is a promise. Its label should say exactly what happens when someone presses it.
Send message, Book a call and Download the guide each say what will happen. Submit and Click here say nothing.
If the button says Book a call, the message after it should say Your call is booked. The same word, from start to finish, tells people they did what they meant to.
